title: Why a buyer abroad just ordered Rs 834 crore of Indian fibre cables
subtitle: HFCL, which runs an optical fibre plant near Hyderabad, has until June 2027 to deliver, as demand from AI data centres lifts the company.
content_html:
Picture a samosa stall in your town. One morning a caterer from another country calls and orders thousands of plates, to be delivered over the next few months. That is roughly what happened to an Indian cable maker this week, except the samosas are cables that carry light, and the bill is huge.

On Thursday, 12 November 2026, the telecom gear maker HFCL said it had won export orders worth about Rs 834.36 crore, or around $88.94 million, to supply optical fibre cables to one customer outside India. The work has to be finished by June 2027. The company did not say who the buyer is.

First, what is an export order?

An export is something made in one country and sold to a buyer in another. An export order is the promise of that sale: the buyer says "make this for me, and I will pay". For the seller, it means money coming in from abroad.

Think of a cricket bat maker in Jalandhar who gets an order from a club in England. The bats are made in India, shipped out, and the money comes home. HFCL's order works the same way, only with cables instead of bats.

What exactly is an optical fibre cable?

A fibre optic cable holds one or more thin optical fibres that carry light, wrapped in layers of coating and an outer jacket. Messages, videos and photos travel as flashes of light inside these thin strands, a bit like a torch signal sent down a very long pipe.

These cables are used for fibre optic communication, linking networks and the giant buildings full of computers called data centres.

Who is HFCL?

HFCL started life as Himachal Futuristic Communications Limited. It was founded in 1987 by Mahendra Nahata, Deepak Malhotra and Vinay Maloo, and today the company is based in Gurugram. It makes telecom equipment, fibre optic cables and other electronics.

There is also a Hyderabad link. The company put Rs 260 crore into an optical fibre plant near Hyderabad, which started work in January 2020, and later added a plant there for cables that run right up to people's homes.

How did the order come in?

Business Standard reported that the order came through HFCL's overseas unit, which the company fully owns. The cables will be made to the customer's own specifications. In a filing with the stock exchanges, HFCL called the buyer a "renowned international customer".

A fully owned overseas unit is like a branch of your family shop that you open in another city. It has its own name board, but every rupee of it belongs to you.

Not the first order this year

This order is part of a run of wins from abroad. In September, according to the same Economic Times report, HFCL signed a three year deal worth $244 million, about Rs 2,329 crore, to supply optical fibre cable to a global multinational company.

Earlier, HFCL also won an order worth Rs 495.8 crore from an international data centre company, to be finished by December 2026.

Why are data centres hungry for cables?

A data centre is a huge building packed with computers that run apps and AI tools. The Economic Times reports that HFCL's big jump in profit was driven by demand for optical fibre cables from AI data centres.

The HFCL results statement for July to September 2026 put this in plain words. Its managing director, Mahendra Nahata, said: "Demand continues to accelerate across AI infrastructure, hyperscale data centres and telecom networks." A hyperscale data centre simply means a very, very large one.

What the numbers say

The demand shows up in HFCL's books. For the July to September 2026 quarter, the company's consolidated profit, meaning the profit of the parent and its units added together, was Rs 394.22 crore. A year earlier, in the same quarter, it was about Rs 72 crore, as the Economic Times report notes. That is more than five times higher.

Revenue, the total money earned from sales before costs, more than doubled to Rs 2,541.79 crore from Rs 1,043.34 crore. HFCL expects revenue for the full year to grow by at least 80%, and says it can reach Rs 10,000 crore of yearly revenue before its old target year of FY29.

The company's order book now stands at Rs 28,911 crore. An order book is the list of orders already won but not yet delivered. Think of a tailor before Diwali with a long list of suits to finish: the work is promised, and the money will come in as each suit is handed over.

What this means for work and money

To make more cables, HFCL's results statement speaks of a planned investment of about Rs 1,800 crore across optical fibre, cable and preform manufacturing. A preform is the thick rod that thin fibre is drawn from, a little like dough that is stretched into long noodles.

For India, each order like this one means dollars earned from abroad for goods made by an Indian company. For students wondering where work is growing, HFCL itself names AI infrastructure, data centres and telecom networks as the places where demand is rising.
